topStories.headline: Supervisors Freeze New Data Centers Citywide — With Bayview Directly in the Crosshairs
topStories.dek: A unanimous Board of Supervisors vote pauses data-center expansion in San Francisco, halting a planned power-output increase at the NOVVA facility on Paul Avenue in Bayview, as a neighborhood biomonitoring group simultaneously launches a pilot proposal to track the campus's health impacts.
topStories.body:
San Francisco's Board of Supervisors voted unanimously on October 6 to impose a 45-day moratorium on new data centers and expansions of existing ones, a measure that takes direct aim at a facility already operating in the heart of Bayview-Hunters Point. The moratorium pauses the expansion of NOVVA, a 7.6-acre data center at 400 Paul Ave. in Bayview, which was slated to increase output from nine to 36 megawatts by 2028.

The measure was first proposed by District 10 Supervisor Shamann Walton and co-sponsored by Supervisors Connie Chan, Jackie Fielder and Cheyenne Chen, and took effect immediately. "During this period, we are looking at issues including energy, water, air quality, land use, and community impacts, while working toward stronger protections and meaningful community input, as well as a data center definition that is clear to everyone," Walton said.

Walton introduced the measure after raising concerns about the environmental effects of data centers and the lack of community input surrounding some projects in his district, which has historically carried a disproportionate share of the city's industrial pollution; existing data centers are concentrated there. During the moratorium, the Planning Commission will assess whether data centers throughout San Francisco, including larger facilities in District 10, pose an environmental threat to nearby residents, studying their effects on water, energy, air quality, land use and the surrounding community. A hearing on the findings is due by November.

The vote came just days before Hunters Point Community Biomonitoring published its own call to action. A massive data-center complex operates across the street from Bayview homes, yet no comprehensive system tracks what its pollution may be doing to residents' bodies. Hunters Point Community Biomonitoring is proposing a one-year pilot to measure toxic exposure, dirty air, noise and heat before the neighborhood is forced to pay the price for San Francisco's AI boom. The data center at 320–400 Paul Avenue was approved in 2014 under an outdated environmental declaration that identified a host of adverse human impacts, including threats from large arrays of lead-acid or lithium-ion batteries.

Sources close to Walton's office say the supervisor hopes the moratorium will result in a permanent ban. The moratorium can be extended to 22 months while officials consider longer-term rules.

topStories.headline: Crocker Amazon Turf Fight Reaches City Hall Steps as Rec & Park Commission Meets
topStories.dek: Opponents of a $50 million Giants-backed renovation of Crocker Amazon Park rallied outside City Hall on Thursday ahead of the Recreation and Park Commission's October 15 meeting, where the contested project is under continued review.
topStories.body:
Keep Crocker Real, the neighborhood group opposing the renovation plan, organized a press conference on the steps of City Hall on Thursday, October 15, calling on neighbors and community groups to rally in a show of unity before giving public comments at the Recreation and Park Commission meeting.

The conflict centers on a proposal to overhaul the baseball and softball fields at Crocker Amazon Playground. With help from the San Francisco Giants Community Fund, the Recreation and Parks Department is proposing a renovation of parts of Crocker Amazon into fields for baseball and softball — five of which would have artificial turf. The Rec and Park Commission earlier voted unanimously to recommend the Board of Supervisors accept a $28 million grant from the Giants; if approved, it would be combined with another $22 million from city funds for a total of $50 million.

The Rec and Parks proposal would require the removal of 98 trees; of those, 23 have been deemed hazardous and in poor condition. To fulfill Rec and Park's two-for-one tree replacement policy, 196 new trees would be planted, and the department said Crocker Amazon's overall tree count would increase by 32 percent, from 309 to 407. Opponents argue that figure obscures a net loss of mature, established trees and that synthetic turf poses environmental and health risks the city has not adequately studied.

Keep Crocker Real has submitted formal public comments to the Planning Commission asking it to recognize that Crocker Amazon Park is eligible for protection under the California Environmental Quality Act and to require a full Environmental Impact Report for the baseball and softball renovation project. Rec and Parks has said it will spend the rest of the year finalizing the project's design, with construction expected to start in 2028 at the latest, and the fields open to the public in 2029.

topStories.headline: Report: Bayview Workers Receive Cents on the Dollar From Projects Built in Their Own Neighborhood
topStories.dek: A new analysis published by the Bayview Hunters Point Coordinating Council finds that residents of the neighborhood received only 4.5 cents of every project wage dollar on major public infrastructure jobs, despite hosting some of the city's largest facilities.
topStories.body:
On July 11, 2026, residents, civic leaders and candidates for District 10 gathered at the Alex Pitcher Community Meeting Room at 1550 Evans Ave. to hear the findings of the Wage and Contract Disparity Report prepared by the newly organized Bayview Hunters Point Coordinating Council. The report was published in the San Francisco Bay View on October 7.

Workers residing in ZIP code 94124 — Bayview Hunters Point — received only 4.5 cents of every project wage dollar on the public infrastructure projects examined. If workers living in the two most impacted southeast neighborhoods together receive only 8.1 cents of every project wage dollar, while workers outside San Francisco receive 23.1 cents, then the question is no longer whether disparities exist.

The neighborhood's infrastructure footprint is substantial. Bayview hosts a huge sewage treatment plant, one of the most significant public infrastructure investments in California history. The community had to pay approximately $500 to use a public room in its own neighborhood to present evidence of how public agencies have allegedly denied the neighborhood a fair share of public wages, contracts and economic opportunity — and after the evidence was presented, those holding political authority offered no meaningful public response. According to the Council, no representative of the San Francisco Public Utilities Commission appeared to answer the community's questions.

The report examines wage and contracting disparities affecting Bayview Hunters Point and other southeast San Francisco neighborhoods, calling for public racial contracting data, meaningful compliance oversight and enforcement.

events.title: CRANE: Shipyard Gantry Crane Light and Sound Show
events.location: Hunters Point Shipyard, Building 101, 451 Galvez Ave, Bayview-Hunters Point
events.description: CRANE is a temporary monument in five movements — for crane, voice, light, sound and projection — celebrating the history of Hunters Point Shipyard and of Bayview Hunters Point, and of the people who built it, worked it and lived it, told in light and sound on the crane itself. Tickets range from $10 (community ticket for Bayview Hunters Point 94124 residents) to $75; the show is also streamed live for free at crane.video.

events.title: We Run Bayview 5K
events.location: Candlestick Point State Recreation Area, 500 Hunters Point Expressway, Bayview
events.description: The third annual We Run Bayview 5K brings the community together through movement and purpose, this year running along the iconic Third Street corridor through the heart of Bayview-Hunters Point. The route starts at Candlestick Point and finishes at the District 10 Health Fest; proceeds support the launch of a Healthy Food Bank initiative for Bayview residents.

events.title: 14th Annual District 10 Health Fest: Bayview in Motion
events.location: Southeast Community Center, 1550 Evans Avenue, Bayview
events.description: This free, community-centered wellness celebration merges movement, prevention, sustainability and neighborhood pride into one exciting festival at the SECC, featuring health screenings, education, entertainment and food trucks; this year's theme celebrates movement, wellness and collective joy in District 10. The event includes the We Run Bayview 5K finish-line celebration and a special performance by Zaccho Dance Theatre.

events.title: Sunday Streets Excelsior: Lucha Libre, Salvi Soul Encuentro & Community Block Party
events.location: Mission Street between Geneva Avenue and Theresa Street, Excelsior
events.description: Sunday Streets hosts the 2026 season finale in the Excelsior on Mission Street between Geneva Avenue and Theresa Street, with nearly a mile of car-free streets. The block party features a Lucha Libre showcase and Salvi Soul Sunday — live music, dancing and art-making hosted by Salvadoran Soul Encuentro — along with other family-friendly programming.

events.title: From The E: Fall Festival Night Market
events.description: The monthly Excelsior Night Market returns for a night of food, fun and community vibes, with unique crafts, entertainment and live music. RSVP to attend and be eligible for a raffle to win prizes, including a themed gift basket. Free admission; all ages.

moreNews.headline: Temporary Green Space Coming to Vacant 3rd Street Lot in Bayview
moreNews.body: A temporary green space is coming to the vacant lot on the corner of Jerrold Avenue and Third Street, where Economic Development on Third Street is partnering with Climate Action Now!, which provides free pavement removal and garden support to businesses and residents near the Third Street corridor. The plan was reported by Mission Local's Bayview Buzz column on October 7. The lot — previously occupied by a KFC/Taco Bell — has stood vacant, and the partnership aims to bring greenery to the commercial strip while longer-term plans for the site develop.

moreNews.headline: D10 Community Pharmacy on Track for Early 2027 Opening at 5668 Third St.
moreNews.body: Last year, the sole Walgreens in Bayview-Hunters Point shut its doors, leaving the neighborhood's nearly 35,000 residents without access to a local pharmacy. After receiving a storefront opportunity grant from San Francisco's Office of Economic and Workforce Development, the D10 Community Pharmacy is now slated to open at 5668 Third St., the former storefront of What's the Scoop, a long-shuttered ice cream parlor. The pharmacy is expected to open in early 2027 and will be located near three senior housing developments. Bayview Senior Services' Cathy Davis and Geoffrea Morris, who spearheaded the D10 Community Market, will lead the effort.

shops.name: Oxbridge Market
